clue.text: Rise, perhaps, to a position in the Opposition

indicators.note: 'perhaps' says the letters of the word before it are only one possible order, so rearrange them

parts.note: a stance is a position, the way one stands or the view one takes

explanation.surface: Someone climbs to a post on the opposition benches in Parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges RISE into RESI; STANCE follows. 'Rise' looks like a promotion, but it is only anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The Resistance is the name given to an underground movement opposing an occupying power, so it is an opposition.

clue.text: Mature epitaph to" an Oriental

parts.note: RIP, rest in peace, is the usual epitaph on a gravestone
E stands for East, so an Oriental gives E

explanation.surface: An older Asian man's words for a tombstone.
explanation.definitionFit: Fruit ready to eat, or a person fully grown, is ripe.

clue.text: If foreign sappers get father …

parts.note: si is French (and Italian) for if
RE, the Royal Engineers, are the British army's sappers

explanation.surface: If foreign military engineers have a child, they become a father.
explanation.definitionFit: To sire is to beget offspring; as a noun it is the male parent, especially of a horse.

clue.text: … his kids'll have to go slippily

indicators.note: to have something is to contain it, so the answer is held within the words before

explanation.surface: Continuing from the clue above: a father's children will have to slide about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'have' says the words 'his kids'll' contain the answer, across the gap between 'his' and 'kids'll'.
explanation.definitionFit: To glide downhill on long runners over snow is to slide along slippery ground.

clue.text: Rising artist at sea is ready to fight

indicators.note: in a down clue rising means read upwards, so the word is reversed

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician, a painter
the Med is the Mediterranean Sea

explanation.surface: An up-and-coming painter on a ship is primed for combat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rising' turns RA into AR; 'at' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone carrying weapons is equipped for battle.

clue.text: Study note was wrong, granted

parts.note: to con is to study or learn by heart
F is a musical note
erred means made a mistake

explanation.surface: A student realises their notes were mistaken, admittedly.
explanation.definitionFit: A title or honour bestowed on someone has been given, as a degree is bestowed.

clue.text: Aid for a bookmaker ?

explanation.surface: A helpful tip intended for someone running a betting shop.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words, the answer is what a punter places with a bookmaker.
explanation.definitionFit: To help someone, usually in wrongdoing, is to aid them; and a wager split in two words, 'a bet', is the stake a bookie takes.

clue.text: People surround extensive property

indicators.note: to surround is to encircle, so the first word goes round the second

parts.note: beings are living creatures, people
long means extensive in length

explanation.surface: Crowds gather round a vast estate.
explanation.definitionFit: Personal possessions are one's property, the things one owns.

clue.text: Fast types, with belts, or those over eight ?

definitions.text: Fast types, with belts, or those over eight ?

parts.words: Fast types, with belts, or those over eight ?
parts.note: things that fasten firmly, such as straps, and drinkers who have had too many, being 'tight' or drunk; 'over the eight' is slang for drunk

explanation.surface: Quick people wearing belts, or the over-eights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast' means firmly fixed, not speedy; 'belts' are both straps and swigs of drink; 'over the eight' is British slang for having drunk too much.
explanation.definitionFit: Devices that draw things firm, or people getting tipsy, both make things or themselves tight.

clue.text: Square parent embraces Irish lad

indicators.note: to embrace is to hug, so the first word wraps its arms around the second

parts.note: taken as written
Liam is a common Irish boy's name

explanation.surface: A conventional, old-fashioned father hugs a young Irishman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Square' looks like an adjective for the parent ('old-fashioned'), but it is the definition: Parliament Square is the London square beside the Houses of Parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: The Westminster open space outside the Houses of Parliament is called Parliament Square, so the clue's 'Square' hints at it.

clue.text: Southwood may hit out

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for south on a compass
a log is a piece of wood

explanation.surface: Someone named Southwood might lash out with a punch.
explanation.walkthrough: The page runs 'South wood' together as if it were a surname. To slog is to hit hard and wildly, as a batsman does.
explanation.definitionFit: To slog a ball is to strike it hard and wildly, the swipe of a batter going for big runs.

clue.text: Classified as Neddy or Edward

parts.note: Neddy is a pet name for a donkey, an ass
taken as written
Ted is a short form of Edward

explanation.surface: Sorted into types, like a donkey or a man named Edward.
explanation.definitionFit: Things sorted into kinds or classes are arranged by type; the word also means mixed.

clue.text: Three played in a Royal Command Performance

definitions.text: Three played in a Royal Command Performance

parts.words: Three played in a Royal Command Performance
parts.note: the nursery rhyme Old King Cole calls for his pipe, his bowl and his musicians three; a king's command made them play

explanation.surface: A trio performed at a royal gala show.
explanation.walkthrough: A Royal Command Performance is a British variety show before the monarch; here the royal command is Old King Cole's in the nursery rhyme.
explanation.definitionFit: In the rhyme the merry old king summons his three violinists, who play at his royal order.

clue.text: Incompetent tripe, badly written, about the North East vote

indicators.note: about means around, so the jumbled word goes round the other pieces
badly written means the word is set down wrongly, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: NE is the abbreviation for north-east
X is the cross marked on a ballot paper

explanation.surface: Clumsy nonsense, poorly penned, on the subject of a ballot in the north-east of England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly written' rearranges TRIPE into IPERT; 'about' puts it round NE and X, after the I.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking skill or competence, someone is unskilled at a task.

clue.text: The trap is clear

explanation.surface: Someone notes that the snare is plain to see.
explanation.definitionFit: A mesh used for catching fish or birds is a trap; and a sum left after deductions, as in clear profit, is the other sense.

clue.text: Miniature mermaid poser ?

explanation.surface: A small question about a mermaid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poser' looks like a puzzle, but here it is someone who poses: a mermaid sitting for an artist would be a scaly model.
explanation.definitionFit: A small-sized replica of a ship or building is built to a reduced ratio; and a mermaid, having a fish's tail, is a model with scales.

clue.text: Expert treatise on a journalist is lengthy

parts.note: a pro is a professional, an expert
a tract is a short treatise or pamphlet
ED is an editor, the usual crossword journalist

explanation.surface: A specialist's essay about a reporter runs on and on.
explanation.definitionFit: Something drawn out over a long time is extended, like a long dispute.

clue.text: Quince with fish to come on stage

parts.note: a carp is a freshwater fish
an actor's stage direction 'enter' means come on stage

explanation.surface: A quince served with fish arrives on the stage, like a strange dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quince' looks like the fruit, but it is Peter Quince, the joiner who stages the play in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Quince in A Midsummer Night's Dream is a woodworker by trade, one of the 'rude mechanicals'.

clue.text: Players who get extensions

parts.note: brass musicians whose instrument lengthens as they push out the slide; 'players' are instruments as well as people

explanation.surface: Sportsmen who are granted extra time on their contracts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extensions' suggests contracts or deadlines; here it is the slide pushed out to lower the note.
explanation.definitionFit: Slide brass instruments are lengthened by the player to change pitch.

clue.text: Black French duck flies back in the sky

indicators.note: flying back means travelling in reverse, so the pieces before it are read from the end

parts.note: noir is the French word for black
a duck is a score of nought in cricket, the letter O

explanation.surface: A black French duck flies home across the sky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flies back' turns NOIR plus O into the answer. The def is loose: the constellation is something seen in the sky.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hunter is a bright constellation of the night heavens, so the answer is found up there among the stars.

clue.text: Lute may be quiet or diminish in intensity

indicators.note: 'may be' says the word could become something else, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: p, piano, is the musical direction for quiet

explanation.surface: A lute can play softly or fade away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may be' rearranges LUTE into LETU, then P is added.
explanation.definitionFit: When rain or pressure eases off, it lessens, slackening in force.

clue.text: Experienced as Pantaloon for instance

explanation.surface: Someone seasoned in the role of Pantaloon.
explanation.walkthrough: Pantaloon is the foolish old man of the commedia dell'arte and of English pantomime.
explanation.definitionFit: A veteran is a person long practised at something; and Pantaloon is an aged figure who appears on the boards.

clue.text: Madly, classically, I love that old bird

indicators.note: madly means wildly, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: amo is Latin, the classical language, for I love

explanation.surface: An admirer swears wild love in the old-fashioned way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Madly' rearranges AMO, the Latin for 'I love'. The moa was a huge flightless bird of New Zealand, now extinct.
explanation.definitionFit: The extinct giant flightless birds of New Zealand were hunted out centuries ago, so it is an ancient bird.

clue.text: Bounces about the permitted area

parts.note: re is a Latin word meaning about, as in letters
bounds are the limits of an allowed area, as in out of bounds

explanation.surface: A ball keeps leaping around inside the allowed space.
explanation.definitionFit: A ball that springs back off a surface bounces, and repeated springing back is a verb in the third person.

clue.text: Russian edict gives this country a direction

parts.note: for a British paper this country is the UK
SE, south-east, is a compass direction

explanation.surface: A decree from Moscow tells Britain which way to go.
explanation.definitionFit: A decree issued by the Tsar or the Russian government had the force of law.

clue.text: "Sport that wrinkled derides " (Milton)

parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Milton's poem L'Allegro, where the missing word is a personified figure who frowns at fun

explanation.walkthrough: The printed dash marks the gap: the line in Milton's L'Allegro is 'Sport that wrinkled ---- derides'.
explanation.definitionFit: Milton personifies anxious worry as a furrowed figure who scorns merriment, the missing word in the line.

clue.text: A farm animal — and no messing !

explanation.surface: An exclamation: a cow, and no nonsense about it!
explanation.definitionFit: Neat is an old word for cattle, an ox or cow; and tidy and orderly, with no mess, is the other sense.

clue.text: How do the heartless show infatuation ?

indicators.note: heartless means losing the heart, the central letter of the phrase before it

explanation.surface: A question asking how cold, unfeeling people display a crush.
explanation.walkthrough: The heart of 'do the' is its middle letter H; take it out.
explanation.definitionFit: To dote is to be foolishly fond, lavishing excessive love on someone.

clue.text: Make ineffective tryst in the dell, say ?

indicators.note: 'say' marks the words as spoken, so it is how they sound that counts

parts.note: a tryst is a date and a dell is a valley, giving 'in valley date'

explanation.surface: Asking whether a lovers' meeting in a hollow can be made void.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' tells you to hear 'in valley date', a lovers' meeting in a dell, which sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To nullify a contract or argument is to strip it of force so that it no longer holds.

clue.text: A proverb hypothetically makes pots of them.

definitions.text: A proverb hypothetically makes pots of them.

parts.words: A proverb hypothetically makes pots of them.
parts.note: the old proverb 'If ... and ans were pots and pans, there'd be no work for tinkers' imagines conditions turned into kitchen pots

explanation.surface: A saying that, in theory, turns something into cooking vessels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hypothetically' hints at the conditional words of the proverb; 'pots' are pans, not money.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb wishes that conditions and suppositions were pots and pans, so they are the things it turns into pots.

clue.text: Loud unruly game

indicators.note: unruly means disorderly, so the letters are put out of order

explanation.surface: A noisy, rowdy pastime.
explanation.definitionFit: A simple board game for children, played with dice and counters, is a popular family pastime.

clue.text: Tax statement involves the Mess in an agreement

indicators.note: 'in' puts one piece inside another, here the jumbled word within the word for agreement

parts.note: assent is agreement, consent

indicators.note: to involve in its old sense is to entangle or roll up, so the letters are tangled

explanation.surface: A tax document drags the officers' mess into a deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involves' entangles MESS into ESSM, and 'in' places it inside ASSENT after ASS.
explanation.definitionFit: A demand from the revenue setting out what someone owes is a statement of the tax due.
